title: One Data Center, One of America's Dirtiest Power Plants
hook: To feed a West Texas data center, Amazon is backing a new gas plant that could become one of the single largest greenhouse gas emitters in the United States.
key_points: Amazon is investing in a new gas-burning power plant in Pecos County, West Texas.
The New York Times reports it could be among the largest single greenhouse gas producers in the US.
The plant exists to power a new Amazon data center — AI demand is the driver.
Grids can't add capacity fast enough, so operators increasingly build their own generation.
Company net-zero pledges and new gas plants are hard to hold in the same hand.
content_html: The abstract cost of AI's energy appetite becomes very concrete in Pecos County, Texas. The New York Times reports that Amazon is investing heavily in a new gas-burning power plant there — one that could end up among the largest single producers of greenhouse gases in the country — built to power a new data center.
extra_html: The reason companies are financing their own power plants rather than plugging into the grid is simple arithmetic: demand from AI data centers is arriving faster than utilities can add capacity, and waiting in an interconnection queue for years is not a plan. So the build-out is increasingly bring-your-own-electricity, and gas is what can be stood up quickly at scale. That collides awkwardly with the net-zero pledges the same companies have spent a decade publicizing. It's worth being proportionate — a single plant isn't the climate story on its own, and your individual chatbot queries are a rounding error inside it. The thing to watch is the pattern: when the infrastructure behind a convenience gets built this fast, the emissions get locked in for decades, and the people living next to it didn't pick the trade.

related.title: AI's Energy & Water
related.hook: Every chatbot reply runs in a warehouse of power-hungry computers somewhere. AI's convenience has a real physical footprint — in electricity, water for cooling, and carbon.

related.title: Communities Are Pushing Back on AI Data Centers
related.hook: The warehouses that power AI need land, power, and water — and neighbors are starting to say no. New York just signed the nation's first statewide data center ban into law.

related.title: Google's AI Buildout Drove a 37% Jump in Electricity Use
related.hook: Google's own numbers show its electricity use jumped 37% in 2025, driven largely by the data centers behind its AI push — a concrete figure in the debate over AI's energy footprint.

flashcards.prompt: Why is Amazon backing construction of a new gas plant in Texas?

choices.text: To supply power for a new data center, since the grid can't add capacity fast enough
To sell electricity to nearby households
Because renewable energy is illegal in Texas

flashcards.explanation_html: Data center demand is outpacing what grids can deliver, pushing operators to fund their own generation — here, a gas-burning plant in Pecos County.

flashcards.prompt: What's the tension between AI build-outs and corporate climate pledges?
flashcards.back_html: Tech firms have made prominent net-zero commitments while funding new fossil-fuel generation to meet AI demand. The New York Times reports this plant could be among the largest single US emitters.
